questions.q: In the worked scenario, which specific hypothesis claim was contradicted by the unexpected result, and which claim still held?
options: Both claims were fully supported, with no contradiction at all
Both claims were fully contradicted, with no part of the hypothesis holding
The relative-magnitude claim (smaller improvement at 5 qubits) was contradicted; the direction-of-effect claim (mitigation helps at both sizes) still held
The direction-of-effect claim was contradicted; the relative-magnitude claim held
questions.explain: Both reductions were positive (direction-of-effect holds), but 0.160 > 0.155 directly contradicts the claim that the 5-qubit improvement would be smaller than the 3-qubit one.

questions.q: What confound did the worked diagnosis identify as the likely explanation for the unexpected result?
options: A software bug in the circuit construction code
The device being used was permanently offline
The 3- and 5-qubit jobs ran six hours apart across a scheduled recalibration, meaning the conditions weren't run under comparable device states
A mismatch in shot counts between the two conditions
questions.explain: After ruling out implementation bugs and parameter mismatches, the worked diagnosis found the run log showed a six-hour gap across a recalibration -- exactly the interleaving failure Lessons 4 and 15 warned against.

questions.q: What is HARKing, and why does the lesson warn against it?
options: A statistical test used to validate quantum hardware calibration
A standard, encouraged practice for writing capstone proposals
A specific error-mitigation technique used in quantum circuits
Hypothesizing After the Results are Known -- quietly rewriting your hypothesis after seeing data to match the outcome, which is dishonest
questions.explain: The lesson defines HARKing explicitly as the dishonest practice of rewriting a hypothesis after the fact to match whatever was found, and recommends a structural fix: referring back to the dated, written Lesson 12 proposal.

questions.q: What structural fix does the lesson recommend to prevent HARKing, rather than relying on willpower alone?
options: Avoid writing any hypothesis until after the data is collected
Refer back to the dated, written proposal from Lesson 12 and report the actual outcome against it, even when it doesn't match
Delete the original proposal once results come in
Rely on memory alone to recall what was originally predicted
questions.explain: The lesson specifically recommends the dated written proposal as a structural safeguard -- a fixed record of the original prediction that can't be silently revised after seeing the data.

questions.q: Of the two honest options the lesson offers for responding to the unexpected result, what does option (b) require if a clean re-run isn't feasible?
options: Omit the unexpected result entirely from the final report
Report the result exactly as it is, naming the calibration-window gap explicitly as the likely confound in the limitations section
Claim the result disproves the proposed mechanism outright with full confidence
Report the result as if it fully confirmed the original hypothesis
questions.explain: The lesson states that if time doesn't allow a clean re-run, the honest path is reporting the actual outcome and naming the likely confound explicitly -- neither hiding it nor overclaiming that the mechanism was disproven.
